\begin{theorem}[Fourier degree under constant shifts]
\lean{FABL.fourierDegree_sub_const_le}
\label{FABL.fourierDegree_sub_const_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_monomial, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_sub, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.fourierDegree_le_iff, FABL.monomial}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$. If the Fourier degree of $f$ is at
most $k$, then the Fourier degree of the function $x\mapsto f(x)-c$ is at most $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Distance from a constant function]
\lean{FABL.inv_two_pow_le_relativeHammingDist_const_of_fourierDegree_le}
\label{FABL.inv_two_pow_le_relativeHammingDist_const_of_fourierDegree_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.Sign, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.fourierDegree_sub_const_le, FABL.inv_two_pow_le_uniformProbability_ne_zero_of_fourierDegree_le, FABL.relativeHammingDist, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_injective, FABL.uniformProbability, FABL.uniformProbability_ne_eq_relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ and $k$ be nonnegative integers, and let $f$ map the $n$-dimensional sign cube
$\\{-1,1\\}^n$ to $\\{-1,1\\}$. If $f$ is not constant and its Fourier degree is at most
$k$, then the fraction of inputs on which $f$ differs from any fixed constant sign
$c\\in\\{-1,1\\}$ is at least $2^{-k}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Variance lower bound from Fourier degree]
\lean{FABL.inv_two_pow_pred_le_variance_of_fourierDegree_le}
\label{FABL.inv_two_pow_pred_le_variance_of_fourierDegree_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.Sign, FABL.distanceToNearestConstant, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.inv_two_pow_le_relativeHammingDist_const_of_fourierDegree_le, FABL.relativeHammingDist, FABL.variance, FABL.variance_bounds_distanceToNearestConstant}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $k$ be a positive integer, and let
$f:\\{-1,1\\}^n\\to\\{-1,1\\}$. If the Fourier degree of its real-valued sign embedding
is at most $k$ and $f$ is nonconstant, then its variance under the uniform distribution
on the sign cube is at least $2^{-(k-1)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Variance bounded by total stable influence]
\lean{FABL.pow_pred_mul_variance_le_totalStableInfluence_of_fourierDegree_le}
\label{FABL.pow_pred_mul_variance_le_totalStableInfluence_of_fourierDegree_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.fourierDegree_le_iff, FABL.totalStableInfluence, FABL.totalStableInfluence_eq_sum_card_mul_rho_pow_mul_sq_fourierCoeff, FABL.variance, FABL.variance_eq_sum_sq_fourierCoeff}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If every subset with
nonzero Fourier coefficient has size at most $k$, and $0\le\rho\le1$, then
$\rho^{\max(k-1,0)}\operatorname{Var}(f)\le\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{S\ni i}\rho^{|S|-1}\widehat
f(S)^2$, where the inner sum ranges over subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ containing $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence outside the dependence set]
\lean{FABL.stableInfluence_eq_zero_of_not_mem_of_dependsOn}
\label{FABL.stableInfluence_eq_zero_of_not_mem_of_dependsOn}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff_eq_zero_of_dependsOn_of_not_subset, FABL.stableInfluence}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and suppose $f$ depends
only on coordinates in a set $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$. For any real parameter $\rho$
and any coordinate $i\notin J$, the stable influence of $f$ at $i$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Total stable influence on relevant coordinates]
\lean{FABL.totalStableInfluence_eq_sum_of_dependsOn}
\label{FABL.totalStableInfluence_eq_sum_of_dependsOn}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stableInfluence, FABL.stableInfluence_eq_zero_of_not_mem_of_dependsOn, FABL.totalStableInfluence}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a real-valued function on $\\{-1,1\\}^n$,
and let $J\\subseteq\\{1,\\ldots,n\\}$. Suppose $f$ depends only on the coordinates in
$J$, and let $\\rho\\in\\mathbb R$. Then the total stable influence of $f$ at parameter
$\\rho$ equals the sum of its stable influences over $i\\in J$.
\end{theorem}
